title: 168 Stairs in Busan: A First-Timer's Guide to the Hillside Staircase (and Its New Free Elevator)
html:
If you've scrolled through photos of Busan online, you've probably seen a steep, colorful staircase climbing up a hillside, with houses stacked on either side. That's the 168 Stairs — written 168계단 in Korean (the number 168 plus gyedan, which just means "stairs") — in the Choryang-dong neighborhood, a short walk from Busan Station. It's one of Busan's most photographed spots, and in 2025 it got even easier to visit, because you no longer have to climb all 168 steps yourself.

A Staircase With a Story

The name is exactly what it sounds like: there are 168 steps, and the whole staircase is about as tall as a 6-story building. It looks steep because it is — the slope is around 35 to 40 degrees, so even local visitors stop to catch their breath halfway up.

This hillside isn't just a pretty backdrop for photos, though. After the Korean War (1950–1953), refugees who had nowhere else to go built homes on this steep slope overlooking Busan's port, because it was some of the only open land left in the city. The 168 Stairs were their everyday path up and down the mountain — to fetch water, go to work, or get to school. At the bottom, there used to be three shared wells where neighbors lined up to collect water back when the area had no running water. Only one well remains today, but it's a reminder that this hillside was a hardworking, close-knit village long before it became a tourist spot.

Good News: A Free Elevator Now Does the Climbing for You

For years, a small red monorail car carried tired visitors up and down next to the stairs. It broke down often, though, and was fully removed in 2023 — so if you read an older travel post that mentions "the monorail," that's why it's gone. Don't worry, it's an upgrade.

In its place, the local district opened a brand-new inclined elevator in March 2025, nicknamed "168 Stairs Sky Road" (초량168계단 하늘길). It keeps the same cheerful red color as the old monorail, but it's quieter, roomier (12 people at a time instead of 8), and — best of all for travelers watching their budget — completely free. It runs every day from 5 a.m. to midnight, so it's easy to fit into a day trip or an evening walk to see the city lights. The ride only takes about a minute, but the view over the rooftops toward Busan port makes it worth doing at least once. It was even recognized as one of the world's best inclined elevators in an international elevator industry awards program announced in late 2025 — not bad for a neighborhood lift!

Here's how locals actually use it: for the grandmothers and grandfathers who still live partway up this hill, the elevator isn't just a fun photo stop — it's how they carry groceries home and give their knees a break after a lifetime of climbing these same stairs. If it's running when you visit, try taking the stairs up for the workout and the photos, then riding the elevator back down (or the other way around).

Explore Choryang Ibagu-gil: Murals, Snacks, and Sea Views

The 168 Stairs are just one stop on a longer walking route called Choryang Ibagu-gil ("ibagu" is old Busan dialect for "story," so it roughly means "Storytelling Street"). As you wander the alleys around the stairs, you'll pass colorful murals painted on the walls of real houses, small stalls selling warm street snacks, and little lookout points where you can watch trains pulling into Busan Station far below. Some murals and photo spots recreate scenes from Korean films and dramas filmed in this neighborhood, so a few corners may look familiar even on a first visit.

Free Korean-English guided walks have been offered along Ibagu-gil in the past — it's worth asking at the small information point near the stairs, since schedules can change. When you're done exploring, it's an easy walk or short taxi ride to Gukje Market and Bupyeong Kkangtong Market, two of Busan's best-known traditional markets, if you want to keep the day going with more food and shopping.

Getting There

The 168 Stairs sit in Choryang-dong, Dong-gu, Busan, only about a 10–15 minute walk uphill from Busan Station (Busan Subway Line 1). Coming out of the station, head toward the hillside behind it and follow the signs for "Ibagu-gil" or "168계단" — there are English signs along the way. If you'd rather not search on foot, paste the coordinates 35.1171295181, 129.0353643591 into Google Maps or Naver Map and follow the walking directions.

There's no entrance fee for the stairs, the elevator, or Ibagu-gil itself, which makes this an easy, budget-friendly stop to combine with a visit to Busan Station or Gukje Market.

meta_description: A beginner's guide to Busan's 168 Stairs: Korean War refugee history, a free elevator that replaced the old monorail in 2025, murals, and easy directions.
